sterling

/STUR-ling/ — 'stir' + 'ling', like the famous silver · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sterling is of excellent, proven quality.

Decades of sterling service earned the librarian a park bench dedicated in her honor.

Worked Example

In fifteen years as treasurer, Ms. Vega never misplaced a cent, filed every report early, and earned praise from three separate auditors. When the board needed someone to manage the new endowment, every hand pointed to her.

Ms. Vega's record was sterling — excellent and trustworthy in quality, like genuine silver. 'Good' work merely meets the standard; sterling work is so consistently excellent it becomes a mark of proven value.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

excellent: Excellent means outstandingly good — top marks for how good something is right now. Sterling adds history: sterling work has proven its excellence again and again, like genuine tested silver, so the word carries a trust that one excellent performance has not yet earned.

first-rate: First-rate places something in the highest class — a first-rate meal or hotel. It grades one thing on quality alone. Sterling praises a record: service or character whose worth has been demonstrated over time, which is why references and reviews reach for it.

exemplary: Exemplary means so good it should serve as the model for others to copy — the word points at imitation. Sterling points at proof: quality demonstrated repeatedly over a tested record. Brand-new work can be exemplary at once; sterling praise must be earned over time.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

shoddy: badly and carelessly made

inferior: lower in quality than others

Where it sits · how far it outshines the rest — solid → sterling → peerless

solid vs. sterling: Solid is weaker than sterling — solid work is dependably good, while sterling work is excellent enough to be held up as proof of quality.

peerless vs. sterling: Peerless is stronger than sterling — sterling means excellent and proven, but peerless means so excellent that nothing else can even compare.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ster-

Root — ster-: star (from Old English steorra, 'star')

Suffix — -ling

Suffix — -ling: small one; one having that quality (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Medieval English silver pennies likely bore a small star: ster- (from Old English steorra, 'star') + -ling ('small one') -- a 'little star' coin, or sterling. Because those coins' silver was reliably pure, sterling came to mean 'of proven, excellent quality.'

Use the root in a new word: duckling

Use the root in a new word: duckling: The duckling paddled hard to keep up with its mother across the pond.
